newsitem.title: HONDURAS: Honduras declares emergency after floods kill 10.
newsitem.headline: Honduras declares emergency after floods kill 10.

text.p: Honduras declared a state of emergency on Saturday in a northern area where torrential rain and floods drowned at least 10 people and drove more than 63,000 others from their homes.
Honduras is one of the poorest countries in the Americas and the government appealed for international aid to repair the damage and rehouse thousands of peasants whose humble shacks were swept away.

"The situation is a disaster. We now face a serious challenge from the epidemics and financial problems that come with reconstruction," said Jorge Aldana, subdirector of the state's Permanent Commission for Emergencies (COPECO).

Aid agencies said crops, bridges and highways were also destroyed by the flooding, caused by 10 days of pounding rains and storms which started to calm last Thursday. They reported at least 10 people, mostly women and children, drowned during the past week.
"The decree of a regional emergency aims to help us transfer internal resources and win international aid to attend to the disaster," said Finance Ministry official Vilma Sierra.
Japanese embassy officials said they will donate $100,000 to rescue and rebuilding efforts, and the Honduran government said it hoped other nations will follow suit.

Businessmen and farmers said the destruction of the nation's banana, coffee and African palm crops, the washing away of more than 10,000 homes, plus highway and bridge damage meant the total cost of the devastation would exceed 400 million lempiras ($31 million).

Six provinces were flooded but the worst hit were the regions of Cortes, Yoro and Colon in the north and northeast of the country. The nation's second-largest city San Pedro Sula, saw rivers of up to 6 1/2 feet (two metres) rushing through the streets on Saturday, two days after the rains eased.
Sports halls, schools and other temporary shelters were overrun with victims, leaving many in the streets waiting for the waters to ebb so they could return to what was left of their homes.
The torrential rain swept away plastic and cardboard hovels near rivers which are home to many poor Hondurans. Even better homes built with brick and wood were destroyed.

The government said it was working to house and feed all victims but many complained aid had not reached them. Long lines of people waited outside food distribution sites in the hope of getting a bite to eat.
As the flood waters slowly began to subside on Saturday, the population faced a possible epidemic of cholera, dengue and malaria because of the mosquitos attracted to the wet region.
Health officials reported two dead from cholera and another eight people sick from the disease. In addition, the floods contaminated the water supply, worsening the risks of disease.
President Carlos Roberto Reina assigned on Friday 70 million lempiras ($5.5 million) to help refugees and begin reconstruction efforts.
Economic Minister Fernando Garcia said the floods were a "hard blow" to the struggling nation and especially to its key exports of coffee and bananas.
Damage to banana crops means up to 3 million boxes of banana exports may have been lost, according to Manuel Anariba, an official with U.S. banana company Tela Railroad Company.
Standard Fruit Company, the other U.S. fruit company operating in northern Honduras, reported similar losses.
